article.title: Rwanda deportation plan revived by five EU states after UK failure
article.author: Nicholas Mwangi
article.content: Five European Union states have announced plans to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda from 2027, reviving a policy the United Kingdom spent two years and hundreds of millions of pounds on before scrapping it. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands unveiled the scheme alongside Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta at the Vienna Migration Conference on November 16. In a joint statement , the governments said they are “jointly exploring” a return hub in Rwanda and aim to conclude an agreement and carry out the first transfers in 2027. As of now there is little information on the cost implications and the actual plan. The same day, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said it had received a request from Rwanda for operational support in connection with the proposed arrangements. Having assessed the request, the UN agency said it could support the hub “in principle, provided its mandate and international standards can be upheld.” It added that it does not take part in forced removals, detention, law enforcement, or security functions, and that any help would begin only once people had arrived in Rwanda. The legal basis is the EU’s new Return Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2026/2280) , which was published on October 15 and entered into force last month. Most of its provisions apply only after a one-year transition, but the rules on return hubs took effect immediately. The Rwanda plan is the first time a group of member states has moved to use that framework to send people to a hub outside the bloc. The plan revives one that collapsed in Britain. In 2022, London signed a deal to send asylum seekers to Rwanda. In November 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the policy was unlawful, finding a real risk that people would be sent on from Rwanda to countries where they faced persecution. The government then passed legislation declaring Rwanda safe, but no deportation flight ever left. The Labour government elected in July 2024 scrapped the scheme. However, the Return Regulation allows return-hub agreements only with countries that respect international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement, the ban on sending people where they risk serious harm. Many doubt Rwanda meets that test. A joint statement from human rights, civil society, and trade union organizations said plainly that “Rwanda fails this test.” UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was “concerned about the human rights risks” of moving people to a country “where they have no genuine connection, and which has its own set of human rights challenges.” Amnesty International called the plan a “disgraceful deportation deal” that “repeats mistakes of the past.” A year of hardening The Rwanda plan is the latest step in a year-long tightening of EU asylum rules . On February 10, the European Parliament voted 396 to 226 for legislation letting member states deport migrants to designated “safe third countries,” even ones they have never lived in, provided the host state agrees. MEPs also approved a list of “safe countries of origin,” including Bangladesh, Colombia, Egypt, India, Kosovo, Morocco, and Tunisia. Center-right and far-right members backed the measures. On June 12 , the Pact on Migration and Asylum took effect after a two-year transition. The package of 10 legislative acts, adopted in 2024, is designed to restrict irregular arrivals and speed up deportations. The Return Regulation followed, and Parliament approved it on June 17, as some right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” in the chamber, and interior ministers gave final approval on October 1. Deporting migrants to third countries has been pursued most aggressively by the United States under President Donald Trump, and the EU has now made it central to its own migration policy. The US has struck such deals with several African states. Under a May 2025 agreement with Swaziland, the US reportedly provided $5.1 million to take up deportees who cannot be returned directly to their home countries. Rwanda itself has separately agreed to accept deportees from the US. The Left group in the European Parliament The Left group in the European Parliament condemned the plan in a statement. “The European deportation machine could take cruelty to a whole new level,” it said. The group noted that the path is currently pursued only by “Trump’s United States,” and argued that the groundwork had been laid by the “safe third country” concept and the Return Regulation. “European countries are negotiating deportations in a market for human lives with no respect for international law or human rights,” the statement said. “Fundamental rights are not suspended at a border nor delegated through a bilateral agreement. We do not accept a Europe that outsources its obligations to make deportations easier.” The group warned that the EU is at a turning point and that “soon we can expect mass raids and mass detention.” It called for “a complete reorientation of EU migration policy: one grounded in human rights and not following the path of a racist agenda,” and ended: “If they expect silence, they will find resistance.” With negotiations still under way, it remains to be seen how the plan will unfold in 2027 amid mounting criticism and condemnation worldwide.
